newsitem.title: USA: Rep Leach hints to offer US bank reform compromise.
newsitem.headline: Rep Leach hints to offer US bank reform compromise.

text.p: House Banking Committee chairman Jim Leach hinted on Monday that he might put forth a compromise proposal to resolve one of the most controversial issues holding up financial sector modernization legislation.

Asked after a speech about his position on allowing banks to engage in non-financial, commercial businesses, the Iowa Republican told reporters he would have a "very interesting" statement to make at at a subcommitee hearing on financial modernization scheduled for Wednesday.
"I'm going to make a fuller statement Wednesday -- I think you'll probably want to wait for that," Leach said.

In his speech to the National Association of Federal Credit Unions, Leach said most in Congress and industry now agree that the 60-year old legal barriers separating banking from other financial sectors should be torn down.
But so far, there has been little consensus about going farther and alllowing banks to move into non-financial commercial businesses, Leach said.

Leach's own proposal for bank reform would permit a minimal amount of non-financial activity in banks. Under H.R. 10, an investment bank could own shares in non-financial companies worth up to 7.5 percent of its consolidated risk-weighted assets.

A proposal put forth by Rep Marge Roukema, Republican of New Jersey, would go farther, allowing financial companies to conduct up to 25 percent of their business in commercial activities. And another bill, introduced by Louisiana Republican Richad Baker would impose no limits.

The Clinton administration, drafting its own bank modernization plan due at the end of March, has also been leaning towards allowing unrestrained mixing of banking and commerce, people familiar with the plan said.
Leach declined to elaborate on his statement. "I will assure you, it will be a very interesting statement," he told reporters. "I've spent the weekend writing some thoughts with some new nuances."
In recent weeks, Leach and Under Secretary of the Treasury John Hawke have spoken out repeatedly on opposite sides of the issue.

As he did before the credit union group on Monday, Leach blasts the idea of mixing banking and commerce as contrary to the national interest while Hawke defends the approach as an important component of financial reform.
